```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Willingness to pay is better evidenced in A. ClaireMed's published $99/provider/month and S10.AI's $99–$500/provider/month tiers are sourced. Even the failure case, Cydoc, landed four paying customers. In B, the only paid-intent signal is one conditional app review, set against at least five free or freemium clones.",
    "Unit economics favor A for a 90-day target. One A customer is worth about $49–$99/month, so a handful of physicians is meaningful revenue. B needs paid installs at about $3.60 each on iOS to convert into $4/month subscribers, with no retention evidence. Artifact, the sector's best-resourced example, saw downloads collapse.",
    "Cydoc's postmortem points to a workable narrow wedge for A. Its first prospect wanted only the note-drafting piece, and psych reports drove most of its revenue. A paste-into-existing-EHR scope avoids the $4–6k per-practice integration cost. B's brief offers no comparable wedge; its niche question is listed as open.",
    "B's core value is described as being absorbed for free into Apple News, Google News, and chatbots. That erodes the reason to pay at all. A's competitors are paid, contact-sales or subscription products, which suggests the category still supports charging."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "The Case For claims Bulletin, KhanList, Content Bite, and Syft are 'single-developer-shipped apps… already monetizing small niches.' The brief gives no source for either their solo-developer status or any revenue or subscriber figures. Listed IAP prices and a download count do not show that anyone is paying. The one demand quote ('Revert the UI back and I'll pay… I'm deleting this') is conditional and describes a user leaving for a different reader.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. A's own demand evidence is thin: a single Reddit complaint about intake paperwork, plus an AMA statistic relayed through competitor marketing. A's Cydoc figures appear without a URL in the brief. HIPAA BAA overhead, liability concerns, and a slow per-practice sales cycle with $3–10k conference costs could easily push a first paying customer past 90 days. B could plausibly get a single $4 subscriber faster, but nothing in its brief suggests that would lead to a viable business. A wins mainly because its pricing evidence is stronger and its precedent did convert payers, not because its risks are small."
}
```
